text: The cache system of doeff. A program asks for a value it has worked out before, and a handler keeps it.
Two effects do the asking. Cache Get asks for the value under a key. Cache Put stores one.
Which cache answers them is not in the program. It is up to the handler around it.
The first call. Cache Get goes out to the handler, and the cache has nothing under my key.
So the handler throws a key error into the program, right at the yield where it was waiting.
The program catches it, does the work, which takes four hundred milliseconds, and stores the answer with Cache Put.
The second call. This time the handler finds my key, and resumes the program with forty-two.
Half a millisecond instead of four hundred. The log shows a miss, then a hit.
Cache Put can carry a policy: a time to live, a lifecycle, a storage, and metadata.
The policy travels inside the effect, so the handler receives it together with the value.
A persistent lifecycle resolves to disk storage. With no hints, the entry belongs in memory.
These are hints, and the handler decides what they mean. The in-memory handler keeps every entry the same way: one with a time to live of a tenth of a second is still there later.
The page's API example. fetch user is called twice, for the same user.
The first call misses, sends the request, and stores the response. The second is served from the cache.
The fake handler got exactly one request.
Now the same program, run twice, under different cache handlers.
The in-memory handler starts empty in every run, so both runs do the work.
The SQLite handler keeps the cache in a file. The second run is a hit, in two milliseconds.
With no cache handler at all, Cache Get is unhandled. The program never chose a cache. The handler does.
Caching in doeff: the program asks and stores through effects, and the handler you install decides where the answers live.
